purpose: Study-only selectable exam-style answer templates for Bocconi Statistics 30001 Chapter 2 and descriptive-statistics crossover topics
warnings: These are student-facing authored study templates, not literal quotations of official model answers.
Use only a template whose stated conditions match the observed evidence; never fabricate statistics.
The 2026/27 syllabus prohibits pre-prepared R scripts and AI during the exam. Study use only unless express authorisation is obtained.

sections.title: 5.7 — Percentages below, above or between thresholds

exam_patterns.verbatim_question_excerpt: Provide a sketch of the graph suitable for comparing the distributions. Based on the graph, report substantive considerations on the differences among customers using different purchase channels.

Do you think a graphical representation of turnover based on a classification into 15 intervals of equal size is more effective than one based on the intervals (expressed in thousands) 8-10, 10-15, 15-20, 20-25,25-35, 35-50, 50-70? Why?
What is the percentage of such customers in the available sample?
Is it possible to evaluate the mean and the variance of the index for the considered posts based on the available data?
Report the percentages of customers who purchased their ticket with an average advance

templates.title: Nominal variable
templates.use_when: One qualitative nominal variable; asking for appropriate graph.
templates.answer_template: The variable [X] is qualitative nominal. A bar chart is an appropriate graphical representation because it allows us to compare the relevance of its categories in terms of absolute or relative frequencies. Alternatively, a pie chart can be used to represent their percentage distribution.
templates.avoid_when: Do not imply the order of nominal categories is numerical.

templates.title: Ordinal variable
templates.use_when: Qualitative ordinal variable with naturally ordered categories.
templates.answer_template: The variable [X] is qualitative ordinal. A bar chart is appropriate, arranging the categories according to their natural order, to compare the corresponding frequencies.
templates.avoid_when: Do not interpret the spacing between ordinal levels as quantitative.

templates.title: Discrete: few distinct values
templates.use_when: Discrete numerical variable taking a small number of values.
templates.answer_template: The variable [X] is quantitative discrete, with a limited number of distinct observed values. A spike plot is an appropriate representation, as it preserves the numerical distances between the values of the variable.
templates.avoid_when: Do not use categorical equal spacing when numeric gaps matter.

templates.title: Discrete: many distinct values
templates.use_when: Discrete variable with many observed distinct values.
templates.answer_template: The variable [X] is quantitative discrete but takes a large number of distinct values. Although a spike plot can be used, a histogram may provide a clearer summary of the distribution by grouping the observations into intervals.
templates.avoid_when: A histogram requires justified numerical classes.

templates.title: Continuous variable
templates.use_when: Continuous numerical variable.
templates.answer_template: The variable [X] is quantitative continuous. A histogram is an appropriate graphical representation, as it allows us to describe how observations are distributed over intervals and assess the shape of the distribution.
templates.avoid_when: If the goal is comparing numerical distributions across groups, consider side-by-side boxplots instead.

templates.title: Compare numerical distributions by group
templates.use_when: Numerical X measured in categories of a grouping variable G.
templates.answer_template: To compare the conditional distributions of [X] for the subgroups identified by [G], we rely on side-by-side boxplots. These allow us to compare the distributions in terms of location, variability, shape and the presence of outliers.
templates.avoid_when: Only assert differences you can observe; include contextual meaning.

templates.title: Approximately symmetric
templates.use_when: Histogram or boxplot with roughly balanced central part and tails.
templates.answer_template: The distribution of [X] is approximately symmetric, with observations distributed fairly evenly on both sides of the centre. The two tails have similar behaviour, and the mean and median may offer a similar description of the centre.
templates.avoid_when: Symmetry alone does not prove a Normal population.

templates.title: Right-skewed
templates.use_when: Longer tail to the right (high values).
templates.answer_template: The distribution of [X] is right-skewed, with observations mainly concentrated at relatively low values and a long tail extending towards higher values. The mean may be higher than the median because it is attracted by the large values in the right tail.
templates.avoid_when: Do not claim mean > median as a mathematical certainty from a sketch alone.

templates.title: Left-skewed
templates.use_when: Longer tail to the left (low values).
templates.answer_template: The distribution of [X] is left-skewed, with observations mainly concentrated at relatively high values and a long tail extending towards lower values. The mean may be lower than the median because it is attracted by the small values in the left tail.
templates.avoid_when: Do not claim mean < median with certainty from visual skew alone.

templates.title: Skew and visible outliers
templates.use_when: Asymmetric graph with several extremes on the long-tail side.
templates.answer_template: The distribution of [X] is strongly [right/left]-skewed, with numerous [upper/lower] outliers. These observations may strongly affect the mean, whereas the median is more robust.
templates.avoid_when: Check outlier fences in Chapter 3 before calling any point a boxplot outlier.

templates.title: Two distinct peaks
templates.use_when: Visible bimodal or two-concentration structure.
templates.answer_template: The distribution of [X] exhibits two distinct regions of concentration, suggesting two different typical behaviours in the sample. Consequently, the mean and median may lie between those groups rather than near frequently observed values.
templates.avoid_when: Do not assert that the two peaks are caused by two subpopulations without evidence.

templates.title: Mean for symmetric numerical distribution
templates.use_when: Approximately symmetric numerical data without influential extremes.
templates.answer_template: Since the distribution of [X] is approximately symmetric and does not exhibit relevant extreme observations, the mean and median provide similar descriptions of the centre. The mean is appropriate for summarising central tendency.
templates.avoid_when: If explicitly asked for both mean and median, report both.

templates.title: Median for strongly right-skewed data
templates.use_when: Strong right skew or upper extreme observations.
templates.answer_template: Since the distribution is strongly right-skewed, the mean is attracted by the high values in the right tail. The median is more robust to extreme observations and therefore provides a more representative description of the centre.
templates.avoid_when: No need to reject the mean if the task explicitly asks to compute it.

templates.title: Median for strongly left-skewed data
templates.use_when: Strong left skew or lower extreme observations.
templates.answer_template: Since the distribution is strongly left-skewed, the mean is attracted by the low values in the left tail. The median is less affected by these observations and therefore provides a more representative description of the centre.
templates.avoid_when: Qualify shape based on observed data.

templates.title: Both mean and median to compare groups
templates.use_when: Groups have different tail behaviour; question asks which measures and why.
templates.answer_template: To summarise the distributions, both means and medians should be considered. While the medians describe the central values, the means also reflect the effect of extreme observations. Comparing both measures therefore helps highlight differences in the shapes of the distributions.
templates.avoid_when: Be explicit about which group has the larger mean/median if calculated.

templates.title: Mode for nominal variable
templates.use_when: Qualitative nominal variable; asked for central tendency.
templates.answer_template: Since [X] is a qualitative nominal variable, the appropriate measure of central tendency is the mode, which identifies the most frequently observed category. The mean and median are not meaningful for this variable.
templates.avoid_when: A variable's codes do not make the mean meaningful.

templates.title: Caution: two distinct concentrations
templates.use_when: Two separated regions of concentration.
templates.answer_template: Although the mean and median describe the centre of the overall distribution, they may not adequately represent typical observed values because the distribution shows two distinct concentrations. Analysing the two subgroups separately may provide a more informative description.
templates.avoid_when: Do not claim the groups have different causes without evidence.

templates.title: A higher location than B
templates.use_when: Medians and/or other location measures are clearly higher for group A.
templates.answer_template: The distribution of [X] for group [A] has higher measures of location than for group [B]. Therefore, the observed values of [X] tend to be higher in group [A].
templates.avoid_when: Do not confuse higher typical value with greater dispersion.

templates.title: A lower location than B
templates.use_when: Medians and/or other location measures are clearly lower for group A.
templates.answer_template: The distribution of [X] for group [A] has lower measures of location than for group [B]. Therefore, the observed values of [X] tend to be lower in group [A].
templates.avoid_when: Confirm with observed plot/statistics.

templates.title: Similar medians
templates.use_when: Medians near the same level.
templates.answer_template: The medians of the two distributions are approximately aligned, indicating that their central values are similar. However, this does not necessarily imply that the distributions have the same shape or variability.
templates.avoid_when: Do not infer identical distributions from similar medians.

templates.title: A larger IQR
templates.use_when: Group A has larger Q3-Q1.
templates.answer_template: Group [A] has a larger interquartile range than group [B]. Therefore, its central 50% of observations is more dispersed, while the central half of the distribution for group [B] is more concentrated.
templates.avoid_when: A larger IQR does not prove a larger standard deviation.

templates.title: A smaller IQR
templates.use_when: Group A has smaller Q3-Q1.
templates.answer_template: Group [A] has the smallest interquartile range. Its central 50% of observations is therefore more concentrated than that of the other groups.
templates.avoid_when: Limit claim to central 50%, not all possible measures of spread.

templates.title: Same central spread, different extremes
templates.use_when: IQRs similar but tails/outliers differ.
templates.answer_template: The interquartile ranges are similar, suggesting comparable variability in the central 50% of observations. However, the distributions differ in their tails and in the presence of extreme values.
templates.avoid_when: Mention the direction and group once identified.

templates.title: Contrasting shapes
templates.use_when: One group symmetric, the other skewed.
templates.answer_template: The distribution for group [A] is approximately symmetric, whereas the distribution for group [B] is [right/left]-skewed. This indicates that the two groups differ in shape, even if some of their measures of location are similar.
templates.avoid_when: Only say this if the plots visibly support it.

templates.title: Q3(A) below Q1(B)
templates.use_when: Q3(A) < Q1(B), both groups observed.
templates.answer_template: The third quartile of group [A] is lower than the first quartile of group [B]. Therefore, at least 75% of observations in group [A] have values lower than at least 75% of observations in group [B].
templates.avoid_when: Never select this template without checking the strict quartile inequality.

templates.title: No substantial descriptive differences
templates.use_when: Location, spread, shape reasonably similar in compared sample distributions.
templates.answer_template: The two distributions have similar measures of location and variability, and their shapes do not show substantial differences. Therefore, the available descriptive evidence does not suggest a relevant difference between the two groups.
templates.avoid_when: Do not claim statistical equivalence or equality of population distributions.

templates.title: Equal-width intervals
templates.use_when: All classes have the same width.
templates.answer_template: Since all classes have the same width, the heights of the histogram rectangles may be scaled using absolute frequencies, relative frequencies or frequency densities without changing the overall shape of the graph. The vertical scales differ by a constant factor.
templates.avoid_when: If area represents proportions, use density so total histogram area equals 1.

templates.title: Unequal-width intervals
templates.use_when: Two or more different class widths.
templates.answer_template: Since the classes have different widths, frequency densities must be represented on the vertical axis. The area of each rectangle corresponds to the relative frequency of its class. Using absolute or relative frequencies directly as heights would give a misleading representation of the distribution.
templates.avoid_when: Never choose the modal class from counts alone.

templates.title: Choose grouping of intervals
templates.use_when: Question asks whether one set of histogram classes is preferable.
templates.answer_template: The choice of class intervals affects the amount of detail shown in the histogram. Narrower intervals may reveal more local characteristics, whereas wider intervals provide a more concise summary. In this case, the classification using [A] is preferable because [specific feature visible in the graph].
templates.avoid_when: Do not assert a universally superior number of bins.
placeholders: specific feature visible in the graph

templates.title: Coarser classes suffice
templates.use_when: Finer grouping does not reveal relevant added structure.
templates.answer_template: Although the classification using [A] provides a more detailed description of the distribution, it does not reveal additional relevant characteristics compared with [B]. The latter therefore offers a clearer and more concise summary.
templates.avoid_when: Only select if the two versions are available for comparison.

templates.title: Long right tail in histogram
templates.use_when: Observed frequencies/densities mostly at low values; long right tail.
templates.answer_template: The histogram shows a high concentration of observations in the lower-value classes and progressively fewer observations at higher values. The long right tail indicates positive skewness.
templates.avoid_when: Use densities, not counts, when widths vary.

templates.title: Long left tail in histogram
templates.use_when: Observed frequencies/densities mostly at high values; long left tail.
templates.answer_template: The histogram shows a high concentration of observations in the higher-value classes, with relatively few observations extending towards lower values. The long left tail indicates negative skewness.
templates.avoid_when: Use densities, not counts, when widths vary.

templates.title: Modal class: equal widths
templates.use_when: Class intervals have equal widths; locate highest count or relative frequency.
templates.answer_template: Since the class intervals have equal widths, the modal class is the class with the highest absolute or relative frequency, [interval]. It represents the interval in which observations are most concentrated.
templates.avoid_when: Do not report exact mode of individual observations from grouped classes.

templates.title: Modal class: unequal widths
templates.use_when: Class widths differ; compare relative-frequency densities.
templates.answer_template: Since the class intervals have different widths, the modal class must be identified by comparing frequency densities rather than absolute or relative frequencies. The highest density is observed in [interval], which is therefore the modal class.
templates.avoid_when: Count height not valid modal criterion for unequal intervals.

templates.title: Largest count is not modal class
templates.use_when: Count maximum is in one class, density maximum in another.
templates.answer_template: Although [interval A] has the largest number of observations, it is not the modal class because the intervals have different widths. The class [interval B] has the highest frequency density and therefore represents the greatest concentration of observations per unit of the variable.
templates.avoid_when: Do not call the highest-count class the modal class.

templates.section: 5.7 — Percentages below, above or between thresholds
templates.title: Proportion at most threshold
templates.use_when: Question asks <= a.
templates.answer_template: To determine the percentage of observations with [X] at most equal to [a], we use the cumulative relative frequency F([a]). The resulting proportion is [p], meaning that [100p]% of observations have values not exceeding [a].
templates.avoid_when: Do not substitute the single-class relative frequency for a cumulative one.

templates.section: 5.7 — Percentages below, above or between thresholds
templates.title: Proportion strictly above threshold
templates.use_when: Question asks X > a.
templates.answer_template: The proportion of observations with [X] greater than [a] is obtained by subtracting the cumulative relative frequency at [a] from one. Therefore, [percentage]% of observations have values greater than [a].
templates.avoid_when: For X >= a with discrete data, check whether the mass at a must be included.

templates.section: 5.7 — Percentages below, above or between thresholds
templates.title: Percentage between class boundaries
templates.use_when: Both endpoints are recorded class boundaries.
templates.answer_template: The proportion of observations with [X] between [a] and [b] is obtained by subtracting the cumulative frequency at the lower boundary from that at the upper boundary. The resulting percentage is [value]%.
templates.avoid_when: Check whether boundary inclusions matter for discrete data or if the class notation differs.

templates.section: 5.7 — Percentages below, above or between thresholds
templates.title: Threshold falls within a class
templates.use_when: Given interval counts but requested cutoff splits a class.
templates.answer_template: The exact proportion cannot be determined from the grouped data because [a] falls inside a class interval. Assuming observations are uniformly distributed within that class, we can approximate the proportion by using the relative width of the relevant part of the interval.
templates.avoid_when: Explicitly say approximate; don't pretend individual data are known.

templates.section: 5.7 — Percentages below, above or between thresholds
templates.title: Both endpoints inside classes
templates.use_when: Lower and/or upper endpoints cut into class interiors.
templates.answer_template: The exact proportion cannot be determined from the available grouped data. Assuming a uniform distribution of observations within each class, we approximate the required percentage by adding the estimated proportions from the partially included classes and the relative frequencies of any fully included classes.
templates.avoid_when: Do not count the complete boundary classes.

templates.section: 5.7 — Percentages below, above or between thresholds
templates.title: Accept or reject percentage claim
templates.use_when: Exam asks whether claim of percentage holds from available data.
templates.answer_template: The statement is [correct/incorrect]. The proportion of observations satisfying the condition is [calculation] = [percentage]%, which is [equal to/higher than/lower than] the percentage claimed. Therefore, the available data [support/do not support] the statement.
templates.avoid_when: Don't use population hypothesis-test language for descriptive assessment of a sample table.

templates.title: Stepwise cumulative function
templates.use_when: Discrete variable, question about cumulative graph.
templates.answer_template: The cumulative frequency at [x] represents the proportion of observations with values of [X] less than or equal to [x]. Since [X] is discrete, its cumulative frequency graph is a step function.
templates.avoid_when: Remember '<= x' includes ties.

templates.title: Ogive for grouped continuous data
templates.use_when: Continuous numerical variable observed only in classes.
templates.answer_template: The cumulative frequency curve shows the proportion of observations with values at most equal to each considered value. Since the observations are grouped into classes, cumulative frequencies are known at the class boundaries. Under the assumption of uniformity within each interval, the curve is approximated by straight-line segments within the classes.
templates.avoid_when: Do not claim exact individual positions inside an interval.

templates.title: Approximate cumulative percentage inside class
templates.use_when: Wanted x strictly inside [a,b).
templates.answer_template: Since the value [x] lies inside the interval [a,b), the cumulative frequency is approximated by adding the cumulative proportion up to [a] to the proportion corresponding to the interval [a,x]. This calculation assumes observations are uniformly distributed within [a,b).
templates.avoid_when: Not an exact count without raw observations.

templates.title: Approximate mean using class midpoints
templates.use_when: Finite bounded classes and frequencies; asks mean from grouped data.
templates.answer_template: The exact mean cannot be calculated because the individual observations are not available. However, it can be approximated by representing each interval using its midpoint and computing the weighted mean of the midpoints, with the relative frequencies as weights. The result is [value], under the approximation based on the available grouped data.
templates.avoid_when: Need a valid representative midpoint for each class; use n if weighting counts.

templates.title: Sample variance and standard deviation from classes
templates.use_when: Finite classes, relative frequencies, n known; asks sample variance or SD.
templates.answer_template: The variance can be approximated by first calculating the weighted mean of the squared class midpoints. We then subtract the square of the approximate mean and apply the correction factor n/(n-1) to obtain the sample variance. Finally, the standard deviation is the square root of the sample variance.
templates.avoid_when: Use n-1 for sample variance, not N and not n; show numeric substitutions if asked.

templates.title: Open-ended class prevents midpoint method
templates.use_when: At least one class has no finite lower or upper endpoint.
templates.answer_template: Since the distribution includes an open-ended class, its midpoint cannot be determined from the available information. Therefore, the usual midpoint-based approximation of the mean and variance cannot be carried out without making additional assumptions.
templates.avoid_when: Does not rule out all other information about a distribution; only midpoint estimates with no further assumptions.

templates.title: State grouped-data approximation caveat
templates.use_when: Question asks if computed midpoint-based result is exact.
templates.answer_template: The resulting value is an approximation rather than an exact measure, because only the interval frequencies are available and the individual observations within each interval are unknown.
templates.avoid_when: Don't call the mean/variance exact without raw data or additional structure.

templates.title: Higher percentage in A
templates.use_when: Outcome share within group A exceeds outcome share within group B.
templates.answer_template: We are interested in the percentage of [outcome] conditional on the two levels of [grouping variable]. Among observations belonging to group [A], [x]% have the specified outcome, compared with [y]% in group [B]. Therefore, the proportion is higher in group [A].
templates.avoid_when: Denominator is size of group A/B, not entire sample.

templates.title: Higher percentage in B despite A counts
templates.use_when: Absolute counts may favour A; B has higher within-group share.
templates.answer_template: Although group [A] may contain a greater absolute number of observations with the specified outcome, the relevant comparison must be based on conditional percentages. The percentage is [x]% in group [A] and [y]% in group [B]; therefore, the outcome is relatively more frequent in group [B].
templates.avoid_when: Don't infer significance from descriptive differences.

templates.title: Similar within-group percentages
templates.use_when: Compared conditional percentages nearly equal.
templates.answer_template: The conditional percentages are approximately equal in the two groups, indicating that the outcome has a similar relative frequency in both. Therefore, the observed distributions do not suggest a substantial difference for the category considered.
templates.avoid_when: Do not conclude independence across every category from one near-equality.

templates.title: Raw counts used in differently sized groups
templates.use_when: Question or statement uses raw category counts despite uneven group sizes.
templates.answer_template: The statement is not justified because it is based on absolute counts rather than conditional proportions. Since the groups have different sizes, the appropriate comparison is between the percentages calculated separately within each group.
templates.avoid_when: Make sure the groups do differ in size if you say so.

templates.title: Higher typical values
templates.use_when: Higher centre in group A supported by summaries.
templates.answer_template: Overall, observations in group [A] tend to have higher values of [X] than those in group [B].
templates.avoid_when: Does not by itself establish causal effect or inferential significance.

templates.title: Lower typical values
templates.use_when: Lower centre in group A supported by summaries.
templates.answer_template: Overall, observations in group [A] tend to have lower values of [X] than those in group [B].
templates.avoid_when: Does not by itself establish causal effect or inferential significance.

templates.title: Greater dispersion
templates.use_when: Group A truly has greater observed spread by stated measure.
templates.answer_template: The observed values in group [A] are more heterogeneous, indicating greater variability within that group.
templates.avoid_when: Name the spread measure used if asked: IQR, SD, or CV as appropriate.

templates.title: Right-skewed spending
templates.use_when: Customer-spending distribution long-tailed to higher values.
templates.answer_template: Most customers spend relatively small amounts, while a limited number of customers account for very high spending values.
templates.avoid_when: Only use for supported spending data with right skew.

templates.title: Similar observed distributions
templates.use_when: Compared distributions similar in centre and spread.
templates.answer_template: The two groups exhibit similar characteristics in terms of location and variability.
templates.avoid_when: Not a claim of statistical equivalence.

templates.title: Approximation caveat
templates.use_when: Using grouped intervals without individual data.
templates.answer_template: This conclusion is approximate, as the individual values within the classes are not available.
templates.avoid_when: Only applies to conclusions depending on unavailable within-class positions.

templates.title: Association not causation
templates.use_when: Observed association, no supported causal identification.
templates.answer_template: This pattern suggests a possible association between [A] and [B], but it does not by itself establish a causal relationship.
templates.avoid_when: Don't assert a causal effect in descriptive observational data.
